Q: Frontend Looks Fine with AI, But Should I Still Learn the Basics Properly? A:

Yes, it is reasonable to build projects with AI while also learning. In fact, this is often the fastest way to get practical experience. However, there is an important condition: AI should assist you, not replace your understanding.

What you are experiencing is a common stage. Many people can make something look good with AI, but the real challenge arises when they need to debug, refactor, optimize, or explain why a component works. That challenge is significant. The goal is not to stop using AI; rather, it is to use it in a way that encourages learning instead of obscuring ignorance.

In my honest opinion, do both, but do not rely on AI without question.

A good approach is to:

- keep building projects with AI

- after every piece of code generated, ensure you can explain it line by line in your own words

- rewrite key parts by hand without using AI

- learn the fundamentals along the way, particularly JavaScript, React state and rendering, hooks, asynchronous behavior, component design, performance basics, and architecture patterns

If you wait to fully learn everything first, you may slow down real progress for a long time. Frontend development is too broad to master completely before starting to build anything. But if you only copy what AI produces, you will remain dependent and your growth will decrease.

The best frontend developers are typically not those who avoid tools. They are the ones who can:

- understand what the tool has produced

- identify when something is incorrect or inefficient

- select the right pattern independently

- debug under pressure

- make architectural decisions with confidence

So your current path is fine, as long as you focus on learning intentionally. A simple rule: every time AI gives you code, don’t just use it. Ask questions: why this approach, what happens if the state changes, what are the edge cases, and how would I build this without AI?

That mindset will transform AI from a shortcut into a learning partner.

Q: argparse with multiple flags and arguments A:

Typically I use the dest parameter of add_argument to specify the variable name.

For example:

parser.add_argument("-a", "--add", dest="add", required=False, type=str, help="some help")

Could be accessed by:

args = parser.parse_args()
print(args.add == "something")

I believe that you need one unique dest per argument.

Also, -h is reserved for help. You may wish to change this to -e or something.

parser.add_argument('-h', '--hello', ...)

Q: Paxos vs two phase commit A:

2PC blocks if the transaction manager fails, requiring human intervention to restart. 3PC algorithms (there are several such algorithms) try to fix 2PC by electing a new transaction manager when the original manager fails.

Paxos does not block as long as a majority of processes (managers) are correct. Paxos actually solves the more general problem of consensus, hence, it can be used to implement transaction commit as well. In comparison to 2PC it requires more messages, but it is resilient to manager failures. In comparison to most 3PC algorithms, Paxos renders a simpler, more efficient algorithm (minimal message delay), and has been proved to be correct.

Gray and Lamport compare 2PC and Paxos in an excellent paper titled "Consensus on Transaction Commit".

(In the answer of peter, I think he is mixing 2PC with 2PL (two-phase locking).)
